title: Voltgrid Engine Assessment
text: Introduction

title: Voltgrid Engine Assessment
text:
What Voltgrid Does
The goal of Voltgrid is to simulate a distributed energy grid at steady state: given a supply profile (available primary energy) and a current grid composition (generator capacities), find the power-dispatch state the network converges to at equilibrium.
At equilibrium, two quantities fully describe the grid:

Dispatch rates \(\mu_i\) per generator — which nodes are active and at what rate they deliver power, consistent with their installed capacities.
Power flows \(v^i_x\) per line per generator — what each node draws and exports, including transfer flows exchanged between nodes and power exported to the external load.

Together these define a complete operating portrait of the grid: not only which nodes are present (capacity) but what they are doing (dispatch) — which flows are produced, consumed, and ultimately available to the load.






NoteWhy steady state?



The optimization does not model dynamics over time. It finds the flow distribution that satisfies all balance constraints simultaneously — the state the network would reach if given sufficient time to settle on the provided supply profile.

title: Documentation of the current core engine
text:
Overview
Voltgrid splits the optimization into two successive steps.
Step 1 — Problem Setup assembles the LP structure: nodes are loaded, balance constraints (\(S \cdot v = 0\)) are encoded, and individual and network dispatch objectives are defined. No solver is called at this stage.
Step 2 — Cooperative Tradeoff then solves the problem in two phases. The need for two phases comes from a well-known failure mode of classic dispatch applied to networks: a single highly efficient node can monopolize all available supply and drive every other member to zero output. To prevent this, GridFlow introduces a tradeoff parameter \(\alpha \in [0,1]\) that relaxes the network dispatch constraint, giving lower-output nodes room to remain active.
Concretely:

Phase 1 (LP) — run a standard dispatch to obtain the maximum achievable network dispatch rate \(\mu_c^*\).
Phase 2 (QP) — fix \(\mu_c \geq \alpha \cdot \mu_c^*\) and minimize \(\sum_i \mu_i^2\), which distributes dispatch as evenly as possible across all nodes.

This approach is much faster than multi-objective alternatives and yields an optimum conceptually similar to fair-share dispatch: each node operates at its maximum rate without diminishing the output of others — hence cooperative. In the absence of additional constraints, the resulting dispatch rates are correlated with node capacity within a network, not as a prior assumption but as a direct consequence of the optimization.

title: Documentation of the current core engine
text:
Step 2 — Cooperative Tradeoff
The LP assembled in Step 1 is solved in two successive phases. Phase 2 replaces the objective in place (LP → QP) before calling the solver again — the constraint structure is not rebuilt.






NoteWhy two phases?



Phase 1 finds the theoretical maximum dispatch rate \(\mu_c^*\). Phase 2 then asks: given that the network dispatches at least at \(\alpha \cdot \mu_c^*\), what is the most equitable distribution of dispatch rates across nodes? The two-phase structure avoids solving a bilevel problem directly.




Base problem — shared by both phases
Decision variables







Variable
Description




\(v^i_x\)
Flow of each line in each node (all nodes combined)


\(\mu_i\)   (objective_[nd])
Individual dispatch rate — stored as a constraint, read as primal value


\(\mu_c\)   (network_objective)
Network dispatch rate, linked by equality to \(\sum_i \tilde{b}_i \cdot \mu_i\)



Constraints







Constraint
Formulation




Balance
\(S \cdot v = 0\) for every bus in every node


Non-negative dispatch
\(\mu_i \geq 0\) for every node \(i\)


Transfer flow bounds
import bound \(/ B\), export bound unchanged (supply-controlled)


Capacity coupling
Stoichiometric coefficient on shared bus \(= \tilde{b}_i\)


Network objective
\(\mu_c = \sum_i \tilde{b}_i \cdot \mu_i\) (equality constraint)









WarningS·v = 0 is never explicit



The incidence matrix \(S\) is never built as a matrix object. It is encoded implicitly by GridCore: each bus becomes a constraint, and each line writes its incidence coefficients into that constraint via set_linear_coefficients().





Phase 1 vs Phase 2

Phase 1 — LPPhase 2 — QP


Objective
\[\max \quad \mu_c = \sum_i \tilde{b}_i \cdot \mu_i\]
Additional constraint (optional — only if min_dispatch is specified)
\[\mu_i \geq \mu_i^{\min} \quad \forall\, i\]
Solver call
# problems.py : 78-82
net.objective = net.scale * net.variables.network_objective
min_dispatch = optimize_with_retry(net, ...) / net.scale
Output → \(\mu_c^*\) : maximum achievable network dispatch rate (min_dispatch)






TipThis is a standard LP



Phase 1 is a plain linear program. Any solver works (GLPK, CPLEX, Gurobi). The result \(\mu_c^*\) is used only as a bound in Phase 2 — it is not the final answer.




Objective
\[\min \quad \sum_i \mu_i^2\]

Minimizing the sum of squares penalizes solutions where one node monopolizes dispatch. It finds the dispatch rate distribution closest to equal sharing across nodes.

Additional constraints
\[\alpha \cdot \mu_c^* \leq \mu_c \leq \mu_c^*\]
where \(\alpha\) (fraction) is the tradeoff parameter set by the user.
Objective construction in code
# problems.py : 53-66
def regularize_l2_norm(network, min_dispatch):
    l2 = Zero
    for nd in network.nodes:
        node_obj = network.constraints["objective_" + nd]
        ex = sum(v for v in node_obj.variables if (v.ub - v.lb) > 1e-6)
        if not isinstance(ex, int):
            l2 += (network.scale * (ex**2)).expand()
    network.objective = -l2   # minimize L2 ≡ maximize -L2
Output → NetworkSolution : individual dispatch rate \(\mu_i\) per node






WarningRequires a QP-capable solver



Phase 2 introduces a quadratic objective. GLPK cannot solve it. Gurobi, CPLEX, or the hybrid solver are required.

Supply File Format
In the pipeline, a supply profile is passed to GridFlow as a packed artifact (zipped archive). Inside this archive, the core data is a CSV file with two essential columns:







Column
Description




id
Transfer line identifier (e.g. EX_pv__D_e for solar import)


flux
Maximum import flow for that source (\(kW \cdot h^{-1} \cdot MVA^{-1}\))



Each row represents one source available in the grid environment. The id maps directly to a transfer line in the network model.

title: Documentation of the current core engine
text:
What is a Flow?
A flow (\(v_i\)) is the rate at which power is drawn or produced by a transfer line. In the context of a supply profile, it represents the maximum quantity of power that nodes can import per unit time and per unit of installed capacity.
The unit \(kW \cdot h^{-1} \cdot MVA^{-1}\) breaks down as:

\(kW\): amount of power (kilowatts)
\(h^{-1}\): per hour
\(MVA^{-1}\): normalized by total installed capacity

This normalization by \(MVA\) is key: the flow value is independent of the site’s footprint. It expresses a rate relative to the network itself, not to the external load.
The conversion from raw supply to flow is:
\[v_i = \frac{D_i \times (1 - A_i) \times 1000}{Mw_i \times B_{total}}\]








Symbol
Description
Unit




\(v_i\)
Maximum flow available to nodes
\(kW \cdot h^{-1} \cdot MVA^{-1}\)


\(D_i\)
Raw supply of source \(i\)
\(kW \cdot h^{-1}\)


\(A_i\)
Upstream losses (before the bus)
unitless


\(Mw_i\)
Conversion factor of source \(i\)
\(kW \cdot unit^{-1}\)


\(B_{total}\)
Total installed capacity
\(MVA\)

section: Supply as a Constraint in the Optimization
text:
Supply as a Constraint in the Optimization
Inside cooperative_tradeoff, the supply profile is not a decision variable — it is a constraint on import flows, applied before any optimization begins (grow.py:55):
net.medium = medium[medium.index.isin(ex_ids)]
This sets an upper bound on each transfer line:
\[0 \leq v_{\text{import},i} \leq v_i\]
Nodes cannot draw more than what the supply allows. This is the operating ceiling imposed on the optimization problem.
The supply profile therefore contributes to both phases:

Phase 1 (LP): limits the feasible space for maximizing network dispatch
Phase 2 (QP): same bounds apply when redistributing flows under the tradeoff constraint

section: Supply as a Decision Variable (Supply Optimizer)
text:
Supply as a Decision Variable (Supply Optimizer)
In supply_optimizer.py, the logic is reversed: the goal is to find which supply profile to schedule in order to reach an operating objective (e.g. maximize reserve power output).

Decision Variables








Variable
Description
Bounds




\(f_i\)
Amount of source \(i\) (units)
\([f_i^{\min},\ f_i^{\max}]\)


\(a_i\)
Addition relative to current profile
\([0,\ f_i^{\max} - f_i^{\text{current}}]\)


\(r_i\)
Reduction relative to current profile
\([0,\ f_i^{\text{current}} - f_i^{\min}]\)


\(\delta_i \in \{0,1\}\)
Binary indicator: was source \(i\) modified?
—





Constraints








Constraint
Expression
Purpose




Source balance
\(f_i = f_i^{\text{current}} + a_i - r_i\)
Tracks net change per source


Max sources changed
\(\sum_i \delta_i \leq N\)
Limits schedule complexity


Change indicator
\(a_i + r_i \leq 1000 \cdot \delta_i\)
Links binary to actual change


Load envelope
\(\text{load}_{\min} \leq \sum_i f_i \cdot \text{kW}_i \leq \text{load}_{\max}\)
Operating feasibility


FBA — balance (optional)
\(\sum_r S_{m,r} \cdot v_r = 0\) for each bus \(m\)
Incidence feasibility of grid operation


FBA — supply coupling (optional)
\(v_{EX_i} \geq -\dfrac{\text{supply\_flux}_i}{\text{FLUX\_CONVERSION\_FACTOR}}\)
Node draw cannot exceed what the supply provides









NoteFBA constraints change the nature of the problem



Without --model: the objective operates on supply flows directly — the optimizer reasons about source quantities and their power content.
With --model: the balance constraints are injected via _embed_network_model(), coupling the supply to actual grid operation. The optimizer now reasons about true network flows (e.g. reserve output as a result of node dispatch), not just supply composition.




Objective Function
\[\min \sum_i \text{penalty} \cdot (a_i + r_i) - \sum_j w_j \cdot v_j^{\text{objective}}\]
Minimize supply perturbation while maximizing the target operating flow (e.g. reserve export EX_res(e)).

title: Documentation of the current core engine
text:
A.1 Optimization Engine
Each section maps an optimization concept to the exact lines of GridFlow source code that implement it.
Base constraints (S·v = 0, objective_[nd] >= 0, transfer bounds, network_objective equality) are all added in Step 1 inside network.py : Network.__init__(). Optimization-specific constraints (individual min dispatch floor, network dispatch bounds) are added in Step 2 inside problems.py : cooperative_tradeoff() and util.py : _apply_min_dispatch().


Step 1 — Problem Construction

Lines → flow variables + \(S \cdot v = 0\)
# network.py : 262-265, 277
for r in model.lines:
    r.id = r.global_id + suffix          # unique namespace per node: "LNK__nd1"
    r.network_id = idx
self.add_lines(model.lines)              # GridCore creates v_forward, v_reverse >= 0
                                         # and encodes S·v = 0 for every bus


objective_[nd] constraint
# network.py : 278-286
o = self.solver.interface.Objective.clone(model.objective, model=self.solver)
obj += o.expression * row.capacity       # accumulates for network_objective
node_obj = self.problem.Constraint(
    o.expression, name="objective_" + idx, lb=0.0   # lb=0 → dispatch_nd >= 0
)
self.add_cons_vars([node_obj])


network_objective variable + equality constraint
# util.py : 205-210  /  network.py : 297-298
def add_var_from_expression(model, name, expr, lb=None, ub=None):
    var = model.problem.Variable(name, lb=lb, ub=ub)
    const = model.problem.Constraint(
        (var - expr).expand(), lb=0, ub=0, name=name + "_equality"
    )                                    # network_objective = Σ capacity_nd × dispatch_nd
    model.add_cons_vars([var, const])
    return var

net_obj = add_var_from_expression(self, "network_objective", obj, lb=0)
self.objective = self.problem.Objective(net_obj, direction="max")


Transfer flow bounds + capacity coupling
# network.py : 323-385  (__add_transfers)
export = len(r.sinks) == 1
lb = r.lower_bound / self.mass if export else -r.upper_bound / self.mass

coef = info.capacity
r.add_buses({medium_bus: coef if export else -coef})  # capacity as incidence coef


Solver selection and Gurobi config
# network.py : 138-143
solver = [s for s in ["cplex", "gurobi", "hybrid", "glpk"]
          if s in gridcore.util.solver.solvers][0]

# util.py : 298-307
if interface == "gurobi":
    solver.configuration.lp_method = "barrier"
    solver.problem.Params.BarConvTol = 1e-9
    solver.problem.Params.CrossoverBasis = 1
    solver.problem.Params.NumericFocus = 2
    solver.problem.Params.Threads = 1




Step 2 — Cooperative Tradeoff

Main function
# problems.py : 70-100
def cooperative_tradeoff(network, min_dispatch, fraction, flows, pfba, atol, rtol):
    with network as net:
        _apply_min_dispatch(network, min_dispatch)     # optional: objective_[nd].lb = min_dispatch_nd

        # Phase 1 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        net.objective = net.scale * net.variables.network_objective
        min_dispatch = optimize_with_retry(net, ...) / net.scale

        # Phase 2 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        regularize_l2_norm(net, 0.0)
        for fr in fraction:
            net.variables.network_objective.lb = fr * min_dispatch   # dispatch floor
            net.variables.network_objective.ub = min_dispatch        # dispatch ceiling
            sol = solve(network, flows=flows, pfba=pfba, ...)
            if not pfba and sol.status != OPTIMAL:
                sol = crossover(net, sol, flows=flows)


Phase 1 — LP objective + solver call
# problems.py : 78  /  solution.py : 214-223
net.objective = net.scale * net.variables.network_objective   # maximize

def optimize_with_retry(net, message):
    sol = net.optimize()           # first solver call (LP)
    if sol is None:
        network.solver.problem.reset()   # Gurobi reset on failure
        sol = net.optimize()
    return sol.objective_value


Phase 1 — Optional individual min dispatch
# util.py : 274-283
for nd in network.nodes:
    obj = network.constraints["objective_" + nd]
    obj.lb = (1.0 - rtol) * min_dispatch[nd] - atol
    if obj.lb < atol:
        obj.lb = 0


Phase 2 — L2 objective construction (LP → QP)
# problems.py : 53-66
def regularize_l2_norm(network, min_dispatch):
    l2 = Zero
    for nd in network.nodes:
        node_obj = network.constraints["objective_" + nd]
        ex = sum(v for v in node_obj.variables if (v.ub - v.lb) > 1e-6)
        if not isinstance(ex, int):
            l2 += (network.scale * (ex**2)).expand()   # quadratic term per node
    network.objective = -l2                            # minimize L2 ≡ maximize -L2


Phase 2 — Solver call + reading the solution
# solution.py : 177-196, 103-119
def solve(network, ...):
    network.solver.optimize()                          # QP solver call (Gurobi)
    if pfba and flows:
        add_pfba_objective(network, atol, rtol)
        network.solver.optimize()
    return NetworkSolution(network)

# reading dispatch rates from primal values
gcs[nd] = network.constraints["objective_" + nd].primal
if interface == "gurobi":
    gcs = gcs.abs()                                    # Gurobi/optlang bug workaround


Phase 2 — Crossover fallback (if QP returns non-optimal)
# solution.py : 237-251
net.variables.network_objective.ub = net_dispatch + 1e-6
net.objective = net.scale * net.variables.network_objective   # back to LP
for nd in net.nodes:
    net.constraints["objective_" + nd].ub = max(const.lb, gcs[nd])  # fix QP dispatch rates

A.2 Supply Math to Code

Part 1 — Supply as a Constraint (cooperative_tradeoff)

Import flow upper bound
\[0 \leq v_{\text{import},i} \leq v_i\]
where \(v_i\) is derived from the site’s raw supply:
\[v_i = \frac{D_i \times (1 - A_i) \times 1000}{Mw_i \times B_{total}}\]
→ grow.py:55 (net.medium = medium[medium.index.isin(ex_ids)])
Active in both steps of cooperative_tradeoff:

Step 1 (LP): limits the feasible space for maximizing network dispatch
Step 2 (QP): same bounds apply when redistributing flows under the tradeoff constraint





Part 2 — Supply as a Decision Variable (supply_optimizer.py)

Decision Variables
\(f_i\) — Amount of source \(i\) (units)
\[f_i \in [\,f_i^{\min},\ f_i^{\max}\,]\]
min_amt = current_amt × (1 − max_source_change_pct / 100)
max_amt = current_amt × (1 + max_source_change_pct / 100)
For new candidate sources: \(f_i \in [0,\ 200u]\)
→ supply_optimizer.py:457 (existing sources) · supply_optimizer.py:468 (new candidate sources)
\(a_i\) — Addition relative to current profile
\[a_i \in [\,0,\ \max(0,\ f_i^{\max} - f_i^{\text{current}})\,]\]
If \(f_i^{\max} < f_i^{\text{current}}\), the upper bound is clamped to 0 and \(a_i = 0\).
→ supply_optimizer.py:460
\(r_i\) — Reduction relative to current profile
\[r_i \in [\,0,\ \max(0,\ f_i^{\text{current}} - f_i^{\min})\,]\]
If \(f_i^{\text{current}} < f_i^{\min}\), the upper bound is clamped to 0 and \(r_i = 0\).
→ supply_optimizer.py:461
\(\delta_i \in \{0, 1\}\) — Was source \(i\) modified? Binary indicator variable.
→ supply_optimizer.py:480



Constraints
Source balance
\[f_i = f_i^{\text{current}} + a_i - r_i\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:475
Max sources changed
\[\sum_i \delta_i \leq N\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:488
Change indicator (big-M)
\[a_i + r_i \leq 1000 \cdot \delta_i\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:484 (existing) · supply_optimizer.py:486 (new candidates)
Load constraints
\[\text{load}^{\min} \leq \sum_i \frac{\text{load}_i}{100} \cdot f_i \leq \text{load}^{\max}\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:991–1004 · supply_optimizer.py:971 (_add_load_constraints()) · supply_optimizer.py:491
FBA — Line flow bounds (optional, requires --model)
\[v_r^{\min} \leq v_r \leq v_r^{\max} \quad \forall r\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:1103
FBA — Incidence steady-state (optional, requires --model)
\[\sum_r S_{m,r} \cdot v_r = 0 \quad \forall m\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:1107–1113 (inside _embed_network_model())
FBA — Supply-transfer linking (optional, requires --model)
\[v_{EX_i} + \frac{\text{supply\_flux}_i}{\text{FLUX\_CONVERSION\_FACTOR}} \geq 0\]
Same structure as Part 1, but \(v_i^{\text{supply}}\) is a linear expression in \(f_i\) rather than a fixed value.
→ supply_optimizer.py:1119–1131 · supply_optimizer.py:500



Objective Function
\[\min \underbrace{\sum_i \text{penalty} \cdot (a_i + r_i)}_{\text{minimize perturbation}} + \underbrace{\sum_j w_j \cdot \text{obj\_term}_j}_{\text{operating objective}}\]
obj_term routing:

With FBA model → obj_term = FBA flow variable \(v_{EX_j}\)
Without model → obj_term = supply flow expression \(\sum_i \text{coeff}_{ij} \cdot f_i\)

→ supply_optimizer.py:507–513 (perturbation penalty) → supply_optimizer.py:515–542 (operating objective, handles RES_total) → supply_optimizer.py:544 (gmodel.setObjective(obj_expr, GRB.MINIMIZE)) → supply_optimizer.py:1037 (_add_objective_term()) → supply_optimizer.py:1051–1058 (FBA path) · supply_optimizer.py:1063–1068 (supply flow fallback)



Supply Flow Expressions
\[\text{flow}_{m} = \sum_i \frac{g_{m,i}}{100} \cdot \frac{1000}{Mw_m} \cdot f_i\]
→ supply_optimizer.py:1006 (_build_flow_expressions()) → supply_optimizer.py:1028 (coefficient computation) → supply_optimizer.py:494 (called from _solve_with_gurobi)

title: Assessing the validity of current core engine
text:
